articles.title: US Open: Carlos Alcaraz breezes past Tommy Paul in straight sets to advance to quarterfinal
articles.summary: Paul has not been able to snatch a set from Alcaraz since 2024.
articles.body:
Carlos Alcaraz is moving on in the 2026 US Open after a definitive win over Tommy Paul, with the No. 2 ranked player beating the American in straight sets, 6-4, 6-3, 6-4.

In a baffling stat, Sunday's three-set victory marks 14th straight sets that Alcaraz has won against the American. Paul has not taken a set over Alcaraz since Wimbledon in 2024, even though the pair have faced off four times since then.

Though Paul was unable to break through again this time, he did put up a fight in the first set: Alcaraz and Paul traded games until the young Spaniard finally broke the American's serve to eventually win 6-4.

Alcaraz looked like he was on his way to an easy win in the second set, but Paul started to battle back, fighting off multiple break points before Alcaraz was able to hold him off.

Paul fought another break from Alcaraz in the the third game of the set, scoring three unanswered points to claw back from a near-scoreless game. But Alcaraz recovered well to snatch the break point and send him on the path to victory.

With Alcaraz one game from a win — and Paul failing to pick up a single break in the third — Paul was able to sweep through his final service game without letting Alcaraz snatch a point back. However, the American couldn't hold off Alcaraz as the Spaniard used his power to deftly finish Paul off.

Alcaraz has barely missed a step since returning from a wrist injury that sidelined him for 4 ½ months. The Spaniard kicked things off with a strong showing , beating Roman Safiullin in straight sets ; though he dropped the first set to Jaime Faria in the second round, he pulled back for another win , and then beat Wu Yibing in straight sets as well.

Initially, Alcaraz's return, paired with World No. 1 Jannik Sinner pulling out of the tournament with a knee injury, left the impression of a wide-open bracket in men's singles . But even after a long layoff, Alcaraz is continuing his dominance: He is now 63-0 in major tournaments after winning the first two sets.

Alcaraz will now continue his journey toward trying to defend his 2025 US Open title in the quarterfinal, facing the winner of Sunday night's match between No. 8 Ben Shelton and Stefanos Tsitsipas.

Paul, meanwhile, will fall out of a Grand Slam before the quarterfinal for the sixth consecutive tournament, with his last quarterfinal appearance coming at Roland-Garros in 2025.

(Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) (Patrick Smith via Getty Images)

articles.title: Alcaraz delivers statement win to reach last eight
articles.summary: Carlos Alcaraz continues his return from long-term injury with a hugely impressive fourth-round win against Tommy Paul at the US Open.
articles.body:
Carlos Alcaraz continued his return from long-term injury with a hugely impressive fourth-round win against Tommy Paul at the US Open.

Playing just his fourth competitive singles match after an absence of more than four months, the 23-year-old Spaniard produced a masterful performance to beat American 20th seed Paul 6-4 6-3 6-4.

He has dropped only one set on his way to the last eight in New York and his quarter-final opponent will be either American eighth seed Ben Shelton or Greece's Stefanos Tsitsipas.

A wrist injury caused Alcaraz to miss both the French Open and Wimbledon earlier this summer.

He had won the previous two Grand Slams - last year's US Open and this year's Australian Open - meaning the straight-set victory over Paul extended his run of match wins at the majors to 18.

Asked on court if he is back to "full power", Alcaraz smiled as he replied: "I think so. Except for one year since [his US Open debut in] 2021, I've made the quarter-finals here. That shows how special this place is to me and shows how well I'm playing every time I come here.

"I just try to enjoy my time on the court and it doesn't matter that I was out for four and a half months - every time I come here, I play my best."

Shelton and Tsitsipas meet in Sunday's night session and seven-time major champion Alcaraz has never previously lost to either player at Tour level, beating Shelton three times and Tsitsipas on six occasions.

"If Shelton were to come through, he is the kind of player that can knock the racquet out of your hand," said American former player Jeff Tarango on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra.

"It's going to be a real test to see how Alcaraz's wrist is with a 149mph serve coming to that forehand, but Alcaraz should get through Shelton if his wrist is fine."

Alcaraz said after his third-round win that he was happy with the level of fitness he had shown in the early rounds following his lengthy absence, while he demonstrated against Paul that the quality of his shot-making is as good as ever.

One sensational cross-court forehand winner early in the second set, which landed in from an almost impossible angle, was measured at 103mph.

That came shortly after Alcaraz had broken Paul's serve in the 10th game of a tight, high-quality opening set to take it 6-4.

Paul, who was attempting to reach the quarter-finals of his home Grand Slam for the first time, battled hard throughout but Alcaraz proved to be too strong.

Paul had two break points when Alcaraz served for the match at 5-4 in the third set, but the two-time US Open champion put together a run of four straight points to seal victory.

Former British number one Tim Henman told Sky Sports: "When you haven't played tennis for four weeks, it seems a lot and you can be a bit rusty. This is four and a half months.

"If you would have given Alcaraz a blank piece of paper at the beginning of the tournament and asked how he'd want the first four matches to go, he would have scripted it exactly like that.

"He's had a few slightly challenging moments but, in the important moments, he's just come up with incredible tennis. That's got to give him so much confidence moving forward."

articles.title: Alcaraz y la magia de Nueva York: "Cada vez que vengo aquí, juego mi mejor tenis”
articles.standfirst: El murciano disfruta de su buen momento y del pase a los cuartos del US Open
articles.summary: El murciano disfruta de su buen momento y del pase a los cuartos del US Open
articles.body: Carlos Alcaraz se mostraba exultante tras regresar a los cuartos de final de un Grand Slam encadenando así 18 victorias en los grandes escenarios de la raqueta. El murciano se siente optimista para lo que viene. Nivel de juego. "Estoy muy contento de ver mi actual nivel de juego. Ganar a alguien como Paul me permite ver donde estoy. Todo ha salido bien en el partido. Lo he visto todo con facilidad. El servicio puede mejorar, pero voy a disfrutar del momento seguro". Sensaciones en Nueva York. "No importa que haya estado cuatro meses y medio fuera, porque cada vez que vengo aquí, juego mi mejor tenis” Sin tiempo libre. "Me he centrado en la recuperación con mi equipo para estar sano de cara a la ronda siguiente. El golf este año no es una opción". Más descansos durante el curso. "Va a depender de cómo me sienta mental y físicamente. Me gustaría tener una carrera larga y jugar 10 o 15 años más por lo que quiero cuidar mi salud mental y mi cuerpo".

articles.title: Wimbledon won't credential influencers, already taking precautions after US Open issues
articles.summary: Influencers and content creators have been all over the US Open this fall, and it's caused some disruptions to the Grand Slam.
articles.body:
There won't be a swarm of influencers at Wimbledon next summer after how things have gone so far at the US Open.

Wimbledon does not plan to allow an influx of influencers at the Grand Slam next summer, according to The Press Association . Security will confiscate items, like ring lights, that could be used to disrupt matches, and Wimbledon will not have any accreditation category for influencers or content creators.

That is in stark contrast to the US Open this fall, which has seen plenty of influencers and other content creators throughout the tournament. That's caused multiple issues already.

While the US Open has traditionally had the rowdiest crowd among the four Grand Slams, the influencer debate has taken off throughout the tournament. Roughly 100 influencers and content creators were credentialed as media this year, nearly twice as many from 2025. A pair of influencers had their credentials revoked , too.

People have been creating content at the tournament during matches, including staging photoshoots and bringing in lighting. Naomi Osaka's first-round match even had to be paused.

While that has brought a lot of added attention to both the tournament and the sport in general, many players have spoken out about the disruptions.

"I feel like it's common courtesy to read up on the sport, especially the etiquette. I feel like it could be a good thing for people to make the sport of tennis popular to their specific audience, but I think it has to be managed a lot better, especially in the situation like in my first-round match," Osaka said after that incident. "Overall, I think there's huge positives. … You want people to continue to grow the sport. I just think it has to be in a way that everyone knows the rules and the etiquette."

There has also been the odor of marijuana, which is legal recreationally in New York, occasionally during the tournament.

"People are allowed to move around in the crowd during points," France's Adrian Mannarino said, via The Press Association. "The tournament puts up with it, and I don't know if it's the best thing for tennis in general.

"There's a smell of marijuana on the court, noise everywhere. The truth is, it's turning into a bit of a zoo."

While Wimbledon is still about 10 months away, the tournament is apparently already preparing to keep things calm in London next summer.

articles.title: Frances Tiafoe Pays Homage to AJ Dybantsa in Video to Celebrate US Open Upset Win
articles.body:
The tennis star showed AJ Dybantsa some love after his Round of 16 upset over Daniil Medvedev at the U.S. Open on Sunday, with the Washington Wizards rookie and 2026 No. 1 overall pick watching on in the crowd:

The two also had a friendly exchange before Tiafoe began a post-match interview:

Tiafoe is a Wizards fan, so it only makes sense that he would find Dybantsa in the crowd. Back in May, he said the former BYU star was his preference for Washington at No. 1.

And Dybantsa was in the crowd at Roland Garros to watch Tiafoe in action during June's French Open as well.

Tiafoe is such a diehard supporter of the Wizards that back in 2024 the team gave him his own bobblehead night as part of the DMV Bobblehead Series.

"I grew up on John [Wall]. I grew up on Brad [Beal]," he said at the time. "... I obviously loved Gilbert Arenas—Agent Zero—he was the man. Antawn Jamison, Caron Butler, all those guys were super cool."

But the future in Washington belongs to players like Dybantsa, Kyshawn George, Alex Sarr, Bilal Coulibaly, Bub Carrington and Tre Johnson. That young core, paired with veteran stars Trae Young and Anthony Davis, has Wizards fans feeling levels of optimism they haven't had since the Wall-Beal era.

And Tiafoe—who will face fellow American Alex Michelsen in the quarterfinals on Tuesday—was quick to show the young face of the franchise some love following his upset of Medvedev.

articles.title: El divertido desliz de Alcaraz en el US Open: "Yo pensaba que jugaba con Medvedev o Tiafoe"
articles.standfirst: Andy Roddick le informó que su rival en cuartos saldrá del partido entre Tsitsipas y Shelton
articles.summary: Andy Roddick le informó que su rival en cuartos saldrá del partido entre Tsitsipas y Shelton
articles.body: Carlos Alcaraz pasó por la vía rápida a los cuartos del US Open y tuvo que atender a algunas televisiones oficiales. El campeón de siete grandes, antes de acudir a la sala de conferencias, se pasó por el set de ESPN, una de las cadenas que tiene los derechos del torneo. Andy Roddick es uno de sus comentaristas estrella y este le pidió a Alcaraz que valorara el posible rival en la siguiente ronda, que saldrá del partido entre Ben Shelton y Stefanos Tsitsipas. Hubo un silencio y le pidió que repitiera la pregunta. Carlitos ha estado tan centrado en su recuperación y en estar listo día a día que pensaba que su cuadrante era el de la parte de Daniil Medvedev y Frances Tiafoe: "Díos mío y yo que pensaba que me iba a enfrentar a Medvedev o Tiafoe". A lo que Roddick contestó: "De nada por la información".

articles.title: Watch Carlos Alcaraz Not Know Next Opponent in US Open Bracket During Funny Video
articles.summary: Carlos Alcaraz was surprised to find out who he would be playing in the quarterfinal of the US Open.
articles.body:
Carlos Alcaraz was surprised to find out who he would be playing in the quarterfinal of the US Open.

The star tennis player was shocked when told he'd be facing either Ben Shelton or Stefanos Tsitsipas during a live interview on ESPN, as he thought he was going up against Frances Tiafoe.

Tiafoe will instead go up against Alex Michelsen, while Alcaraz will have to wait until later on Sunday for his opponent to be decided.

No matter who he faces, Alcaraz will be the presumed favorite. The defending US Open champion has thrived in his return to tennis after several months off, losing just one set in his first four matches in New York.

He beat Tommy Paul 6-4, 6-3, 6-4 on Sunday to advance to the quarterfinal, and he'll look to carry his momentum into his next match, which will be on Tuesday.

Luckily for Alcaraz, he was informed of his potential opponent before Sunday's match between Shelton and Tsitsipas, so he'll have the chance to watch and prepare for his next match.

articles.title: Who are Iga Swiatek’s parents? Meet Tomasz Swiatek, Olympic rower dad, and orthodontist mom Dorota
articles.summary: International Sports News: Iga Swiatek’s rise to the top of women’s tennis has been shaped by a family with sporting and professional roots. Her father, Tomasz Swiatek, represen.
articles.body: Iga Swiatek’s rise to the top of women’s tennis has been shaped by a family with sporting and professional roots. Her father, Tomasz Swiatek, represented Poland in rowing at the 1988 Seoul Olympics, while her mother, Dorota Swiatek, built a career as an orthodontist. Iga has also credited her older sister, Agata Swiatek, with inspiring her to pick up tennis. From sibling rivalry to years of coaching from her father, the family played a role in her development. Here’s a closer look at Iga Swiatek’s parents, sister and the influence they had on her career.Tomasz Swiatek shaped Iga’s sporting pathTomasz Swiatek was an accomplished athlete before his daughter became one of tennis’s biggest names. He competed for Poland in the men’s quadruple sculls at the 1988 Summer Olympics in Seoul. His experience in elite sport gave him an understanding of training, discipline and competition, which later became useful as Iga developed her own career.Tomasz encouraged both of his daughters, Agata and Iga, to become involved in sport. However, he wanted them to choose an individual discipline rather than a team sport. Iga initially tried swimming but did not enjoy it because she was afraid of the water. Tennis soon became the better fit.In interviews, Iga has explained that her older sister played a key role in that decision. Agata, who is three years older, was already playing tennis, and Iga wanted to follow her example. Their competitive relationship also pushed Iga forward. She recalled that she often competed with Agata when they were younger and usually lost, which gave her extra motivation to improve.Iga eventually turned that early rivalry into a professional career. She started playing tennis at around six or seven and quickly showed the ability to compete at a high level. In 2020, she made history by becoming the first Polish player to win a Grand Slam singles title when she captured the French Open.Tomasz remained closely involved throughout much of that journey. He served as the head of Iga’s coaching team until 2024, before stepping back to give his daughter greater independence. Even after leaving that formal role, he has continued to support her at tournaments and speak publicly about her career.Dorota and Agata built careers away from tennisWhile Tomasz and Iga became closely associated with competitive sport, Dorota Swiatek followed a different professional path. She is an orthodontist and has worked in the field since 1991. Her professional work focuses on orthodontic treatment, including dental alignment problems and other defects.Dorota has also emphasized that her daughter’s happiness matters more to her than trophies. In a 2020 interview with Polish outlet Super Express, she said she was proud of Iga’s achievements but cared most about seeing her do something she genuinely loved. She was also not shocked by Iga’s breakthrough at the 2020 French Open, having watched her development for many years.Agata followed their mother into the medical profession. After playing junior tennis, she stopped competing around 2015-2016 after an injury. She later graduated from the Medical University of Lublin in 2022 and began working as a dentist, with an interest in periodontology.Despite taking different professional paths, the Swiatek family has remained closely connected. Iga’s story shows how her parents provided support in different ways, while her sister’s example helped spark the competitive drive that eventually took her to the biggest stages in tennis.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Who are Jessica Pegula’s parents? Meet billionaire dad Terry and Kim Pegula, the family behind her tennis career
articles.summary: International Sports News: Jessica Pegula’s tennis career has been backed by two parents who built very different lives before becoming known around the sports world. Her father.
articles.body: Jessica Pegula’s tennis career has been backed by two parents who built very different lives before becoming known around the sports world. Her father, Terry Pegula, made his fortune in oil and gas before becoming the owner of the Buffalo Bills and Buffalo Sabres. Her mother, Kim Pegula, was born in South Korea and adopted by a New York family as a child before building a career in sports. The couple encouraged Jessica to play tennis from age seven and moved their family to support her training. Their support has remained important throughout her career.Terry and Kim Pegula supported Jessica Pegula’s tennis from an early ageTerry and Kim began encouraging Jessica to play tennis when she was 7. She was born in Buffalo, N.Y., and the family later moved to Wexford, Pa., South Carolina and Florida as Jessica focused more seriously on the sport.Jessica has said her parents put her tennis ahead of their connection to professional sports. Kim summed up that attitude in a 2019 interview with WKBW-TV after Jessica won the Citi Open.“We always say she’s our first sports team and our favorite,” Kim said.Terry studied petroleum and natural gas engineering at Penn State before working in the oil industry. In 1983, he started East Resources after borrowing $7,500 from family and friends. He later sold most of the company’s assets to Royal Dutch Shell for $4.7 billion in 2010, according to Forbes.The Pegulas then moved into professional sports. They bought the Buffalo Sabres in 2011 and became owners of the Buffalo Bills in 2014.Kim’s story is very different. She was born in Seoul and was adopted by Ralph and Marilyn Kerr when she was 5. She grew up in Fairport, N.Y., and graduated from Houghton College in 1991 with a communications degree.Jessica has also spoken about how her parents handled her tennis career. In a 2021 Bills Pod Squad interview, she described Terry as “old school” and said he always pushed her to work harder. She described Kim as more focused on life away from the court, including diet, recovery and training.Kim Pegula’s journey and her family’s support for JessicaKim’s background has also shaped Jessica’s connection to her heritage. After winning the 2023 Korea Open in Seoul, Jessica wrote on X that the victory was “extra special” because she is half Korean. She said she was still learning about her culture and was moved by the support from Korean fans.The family went through a difficult period in 2022 when Kim suffered cardiac arrest. Jessica later wrote in The Players’ Tribune that her family spent about two weeks at the hospital and that Terry stayed close to Kim during her recovery. NHL.com also reported on Jessica’s 2023 update about her mother’s recovery.Jessica has been clear that her parents’ influence was not simply about money or access to sports. “My parents have helped me achieve this dream I am living,” she wrote. “Even though we didn’t always agree, they pushed me, and I pushed back, and it got me to where I am today.”They gave Jessica the chance to pursue tennis, pushed her when needed and supported her away from the court. Jessica went on to become one of the leading American players of her generation, while her parents remained closely connected to her journey.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Newspaper headlines: 'Losing battle to halt Russia's 'hybrid' war' and 'Oh chute!'
articles.summary: A warning from defence officials and a skydiving miracle lead Monday's front pages.
articles.body:
The Daily Telegraph reports that the British Chambers of Commerce has called for the pension triple lock to be scrapped in a bid to help, what the paper refers to as, Britain's "ailing economy". The business group, which represents more than 65,000 firms, suggests the savings should be used to tackle youth unemployment.

The Financial Times carries a warning from intelligence officials that Europe is "losing the battle" to stop Russia's "hybrid" war against the continent. Experts say last month's failed drone attack on Leipzig airport should serve as a "wake up call". Moscow has denied any involvement.

"Just 1% of asylum pleas are genuine", is the headline on the front page of the Times. An anonymous whistleblower, described as a Home Office official, has told the paper that asylum seekers from certain countries are using the "same script". The Home Office says asylum claims are considered on an individual basis, and processes are in place to assess their credibility.

The i Paper leads on the former Labour cabinet minister Lord Blunkett, who's urging Andy Burnham to "find the money to fund end-of-life care ". He's joined a call, backed by almost 300 MPs and peers, to boost funding for hospices, which are facing a £745m gap. The Department of Health has previously said it will continue to support hospices.

According to the Daily Telegraph the " scourge of the tennis influencer " will not be coming to Wimbledon. The All England Club is set to take a stand, after various distractions at the US Open. These have included people taking photographs using bright lighting, and too much noise during points, much to the annoyance of players.

And a couple of the papers report on a museum in the United States revealing its latest acquisition, red leather sofas once used by visitors to the National Gallery in London. The Daily Telegraph and the Times both say the pieces were sold after being deemed a fire risk, and difficult to clean. But it hasn't stopped the Wadsworth Atheneum in Connecticut proudly posting a photograph of its new furnishings, with the caption "your seat awaits".

images.caption: Defence officials tell the Financial Times that Europe is losing a "battle to halt Russia's 'hybrid' war" against the continent after the foiled Leipzig/Halle airport attack in Germany. They have called for it to "rapidly develop new methods to suppress Moscow's campaign against Nato member states or risk escalation". Also on the paper's front page, it reports that the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is on course to win a regional election. It says the right-wing AfD is projected to become the largest party in Saxony-Anhalt but is expected to fall short of a parliamentary majority.

articles.title: Inspiring story of the day: “My grandfather always told me to focus on the Three Cs: Cabeza, Corazón y Cojones” - How Carlos Alcaraz turned three generations of family love into tennis immortality
articles.summary: International Sports News: Carlos Alcaraz’s rise to seven Grand Slam titles has been shaped by more than his talent on the tennis court. A lesson from his grandfather, Carlos Al.
articles.body: Carlos Alcaraz’s rise to seven Grand Slam titles has been shaped by more than his talent on the tennis court. A lesson from his grandfather, Carlos Alcaraz Lerma, became one of the most personal parts of his career: “Cabeza, corazón y cojones” - head, heart and courage. Alcaraz later had the three Cs tattooed on his wrist as a reminder of that message. His close relationship with former world No. 1 Juan Carlos Ferrero also played a major role in his development. Together, those family and coaching ties helped shape the player who became the youngest man to complete the Career Grand Slam in 2026.What did Carlos Alcaraz’s grandfather teach him about the Three CsThe phrase came from Alcaraz’s grandfather and stayed with him as he grew up in El Palmar, Murcia. The three words are “Cabeza, corazón y cojones”, which mean head, heart and courage, with the final Spanish word being a much stronger and more informal expression.For Alcaraz, the idea was simple. He needed his head to make the right decisions, his heart to play with passion and courage to take risks when the pressure was highest.Alcaraz has spoken about the message before, saying:“My grandfather always told me to focus on the Three Cs: head, heart, and balls.”The words became closely linked with his identity as a player. His tennis is built around attacking shots, quick movement and a willingness to try difficult plays even when a match is going against him.The story also has a strong family connection. Alcaraz’s grandfather was involved with tennis in El Palmar, where the young player spent part of his early years around the sport.That makes the “Three Cs” more than a slogan. It is a piece of advice that Alcaraz has carried from his childhood into the biggest matches of his career.Why did Carlos Alcaraz get the Three Cs tattooAfter breaking through at the highest level, Alcaraz chose to keep his grandfather’s message with him permanently. In 2022, he got a CCC tattoo, representing “Cabeza, Corazón y Cojones.”The tattoo became a visible reminder of the words that had followed him through his early tennis career. Reports at the time said the tattoo was placed on his wrist and was connected directly to his grandfather’s motto.The timing was also significant. Alcaraz had just enjoyed the breakthrough season that changed his career. He won his first Masters 1000 title in Miami in April 2022 and then won his first Grand Slam at the US Open later that year.By September 2022, he had also become the youngest player to reach No. 1 in the ATP rankings at 19 years and four months. He finished that season as the youngest year-end No. 1 in ATP history.The tattoo therefore came during the period when Alcaraz was moving from a highly rated teenager to one of the biggest names in tennis.Rather than choosing a trophy or a tournament date, he picked something tied to his family.How did Juan Carlos Ferrero become like a second father to Carlos AlcarazAlcaraz’s grandfather gave him the message, but Juan Carlos Ferrero became one of the most important people in turning that young talent into a top-level player.Ferrero, a former world No. 1 and 2003 French Open champion, began working with Alcaraz when the Spaniard was a teenager. Alcaraz trained at Ferrero’s academy in Villena, Spain, and their relationship grew far beyond normal coach-player duties.Alcaraz has openly described Ferrero as his mentor and second father.“He was my mentor. Everything that I’ve done is thanks to him. I learned a lot, not only professionally, but the personal part as well. He’s my second father… I am the person and the player I am today thanks to him.”Those comments came after years of working together. Ferrero also described Alcaraz as being like a fourth child to him, showing how close the relationship had become.One of the most emotional moments in their relationship came in 2022. Ferrero’s father, Eduardo Ferrero, died suddenly in March while Juan Carlos was in the United States with Alcaraz. Ferrero returned to Spain for the funeral before coming back to Miami, where Alcaraz was preparing for the tournament final.Alcaraz went on to beat Casper Ruud 7-5, 6-4 in the Miami final to win his first Masters 1000 title. Afterward, the two shared an emotional moment.Their professional partnership eventually ended in December 2025 after about seven years. Even then, Alcaraz made clear how much Ferrero had meant to his career, calling their time together an important chapter of his life.How have Carlos Alcaraz’s family lessons followed him into tennis historyThe clearest proof of Alcaraz’s growth came in 2026.He entered the Australian Open without a title at Melbourne Park, but defeated Novak Djokovic in the final to win his seventh Grand Slam. That victory completed all four major titles for Alcaraz: the US Open, Wimbledon, Roland Garros and Australian Open.At 22 years and 272 days, he became the youngest man to complete the Career Grand Slam in the Open Era.His Grand Slam record now includes two US Open titles, two Wimbledon titles, two French Open titles and one Australian Open title.Even with those achievements, the idea behind the Three Cs remains easy to understand. Head is about making good decisions. Heart is about loving the game. Courage is about taking the shot when the moment demands it.That message began with his grandfather and became part of Alcaraz’s identity long before he was winning major trophies. His tattoo keeps those words close, while the years with Ferrero helped him learn how to handle the pressure that comes with becoming a champion.And now, at 23, Alcaraz is already a seven-time major winner and a Career Grand Slam champion. His records have grown, but the family lesson behind the three letters has stayed remarkably simple.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: El arte en peligro de extinción en el tenis: el revés a una mano desaparece 150 años después
articles.standfirst: Por primera vez en 150 años ningún jugador con revés a una mano alcanzará las semifinales de un Grand Slam
articles.summary: Por primera vez en 150 años ningún jugador con revés a una mano alcanzará las semifinales de un Grand Slam
articles.body: Con la eliminación del griego Stefanos Tsitsipas en los octavos de final del Abierto de Estados Unidos ante Ben Shelton, ya es seguro que, por primera vez en 150 años, ningún jugador con revés a una mano alcanzará las semifinales de un Grand Slam. "Tengo una racha de 150 años que salvar", escribió recientemente Tsitsipas en sus redes sociales, al referirse a este dato y al 'peligro de extinción' del revés a una mano. No pudo hacerlo. Se rindió por 6-2, 6-3 y 6-4 ante Ben Shelton, que será el próximo rival del español Carlos Alcaraz en los cuartos de final. Tsitsipas es uno de los cada vez menos jugadores del circuito ATP que utilizan el revés a una mano. Se une al italiano Lorenzo Musetti, el canadiense Denis Shapovalov y el búlgaro Grigor Dimitrov, todos ya eliminados en Nueva York. Hasta el legendario Roger Federer, que hizo maravillas con su icónico revés a una mano, analizó la crisis de este golpe. "Me encanta ver cuando a los jugadores de revés a una mano les va bien. Cuando crecía, diría que el 90% de mis entrenadores tenían revés a una mano. Creo que, cuando tu entrenador juega el revés a una mano, es muy probable que tú también acabes jugándolo así. Hoy en día, probablemente la mayoría de los entrenadores juegan el revés a dos manos, y es más fácil enseñarle a un niño a golpear el revés con dos manos", reflexionó. "Luego hay que sumar la tecnología de las raquetas y de las cuerdas, quizá la lentitud de las pelotas y de las pistas hoy en día, y el hecho de que posiblemente se trabaja menos la transición y menos las voleas. En mi época, quizá hacía un 50-50 entre voleas y juego en la red, y juego desde el fondo de pista. Antes de mi tiempo, probablemente era un 80% de juego en la red y un 20% de ejercicios desde el fondo, y ahora es como un 90-10, ¿no?, prácticamente todo desde el fondo", continuó. "Por eso creo que el revés a dos manos te permite, especialmente con la posición abierta y los deslizamientos, como hemos visto hacer a Rafa y a Novak, defender de una forma increíble por ese lado. Antes teníamos la sensación de que, con dos manos, quedabas más corto en el lado del revés y que el revés a una mano suponía una ventaja ahí, algo que parece que ya no es necesariamente así", insistió

articles.title: A qué hora y dónde ver el Alcaraz - Shelton: horario y canal de TV de los cuartos del US Open
articles.standfirst: El español ha ganado los tres precedentes con el estadounidense, el último de ellos en Roland Garros 2025
articles.summary: El español ha ganado los tres precedentes con el estadounidense, el último de ellos en Roland Garros 2025
articles.body: Carlos Alcaraz se enteró a última hora de la noche del domingo que su rival en los cuartos del US Open será el local Ben Shelton. El número nueve mundial y octavo cabeza de serie del cuadro se deshizo de Stefanos Tsitsipas en la ronda de octavos. Shelton ha cedido los tres precedentes con el murciano, el último de ellos en los octavos de Roland Garros 2025. El estadounidense viene en forma como lo demuestra su título en el Masters 1000 de Montreal en el inicio de la gira americana de pista dura. Su mejor resultado en el cuarto grande del calendario fueron las semifinales de 2023. El partido de cuartos del US Open entre Carlos Alcaraz y Ben Shelton se disputará este martes 8 de septiembre en la central Arthur Ashe, del Billie Jean King Tennis Center, en la sesión nocturna, en un horario todavía por confirmar. El partido entre Carlos Alcaraz y Ben Shelton de los cuartos del US Open se podrá ver en Movistar+. También podrás seguir la última hora y todo lo que ocurra en el encuentro a través de MARCA.com y Radio MARCA.

articles.title: El último reto de Jaime Alcaraz a su hermano Carlitos: una celebración al estilo 'Son Goku'
articles.standfirst: El favorito del público neoyorquino volvió a innovar a la conclusión de los octavos con Paul
articles.summary: El favorito del público neoyorquino volvió a innovar a la conclusión de los octavos con Paul
articles.body: Cuando terminan las exhibiciones de Carlos Alcaraz en la pista Arthur Ashe, la central más grande del planeta tenis, todos los asistentes permanecen sentados en sus sillas. Esperan ver cómo celebra sus triunfos el campeón de siete grandes. Alcaraz, que en la segunda y la tercera ronda, imitó a un arquero, al más puro estilo 'Robin Hodd', se acordó tras ganar a Tommy Paul de 'Son Goku'. Era con motivo del último reto que le había planteado su hermano pequeño Jaime. El tenista de El Palmar, a sus 23 años, se ha convertido en el jugador con un mayor porcentaje de partidos ganados en el Abierto de los Estados Unidos en la Era Open. Alcanza el 93 por ciento de efectividad.

articles.title: Sabalenka overcomes tricky Townsend test at US Open
articles.summary: Two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka emulates Serena Williams by overcoming Taylor Townsend to reach a sixth straight US Open quarter-final.
articles.body:
Two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka emulated Serena Williams as she eventually overpowered American Taylor Townsend to reach a sixth straight US Open quarter-final.

A topsy-turvy contest featured 10 breaks of serve, but Sabalenka recovered from 3-1 down in the second set to seal a 6-4 6-3 victory with a fifth consecutive game.

It was the Belarusian's 18th consecutive win at the tournament, extending her three-year unbeaten streak following back-to-back triumphs in 2024 and 2025.

Sabalenka, 28, is the first woman to reach six consecutive singles quarter-finals at Flushing Meadows since American great Williams in 2016.

Six-time champion Williams was also the last player to win three US Open titles in a row, and Sabalenka is now three wins from matching that feat.

She will face Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova for a semi-final place, after the Czech sixth seed required six match points to overcome Ukraine's Marta Kostyuk in a rollercoaster 7-5 5-7 6-4 win.

Despite the straightforward scoreline this was a tricky match which required a resilient display from Sabalenka, who also had the vast majority of the crowd against her.

In that context this was an impressive victory for the four-time major winner, who has not always managed to maintain her composure in similarly testing scenarios.

"I was just trying to stay focused on myself, not only point by point but ball by ball," Sabalenka said.

"I'm happy I was able to turn around the second set, I think it was a key moment."

The match began with five successive breaks of serve - mostly due to excellent returning by both players - but it was Sabalenka who finally took charge.

Doubles specialist Townsend, who walked out wearing a long, black-feathered outfit, continued to frustrate Sabalenka and forced her to serve out the set at the second opportunity, before making the breakthrough in the second set.

But Sabalenka, aware she must lift the trophy to have a chance of retaining her number one ranking, produced an immediate reply as she broke back to love and dashed to the finish line, wrapping up the victory in 75 minutes.

Pegula wins to bring curtain down on Cirstea's Grand Slam career

American third seed Jessica Pegula brought the curtain down on Sorana Cirstea's Grand Slam career with a 6-3 6-4 win over the Romanian.

Cirstea is set to retire at the end of 2026, despite it being one of the best seasons of her 20-year career.

In May, the 36-year-old became the oldest player in rankings history to make her top 20 debut and she is currently ranked at a career-high 17th following a run to the quarter-finals at the French Open.

She also reached the third round at the Australian Open and Wimbledon, while she lifted the fourth WTA title of her career at her home tournament in Cluj-Napoca.

But Cirstea missed out on a third major quarter-final as Pegula came through a tricky test that saw 11 breaks of serve, securing victory on her third match point.

"I just told her I don't know if you're still going to play next year, but you are playing great and I said I have a lot of respect for you," Pegula said when asked what she told Cirstea when they shared an embrace at the net.

Pegula, the 2024 runner-up to Sabalenka, will continue her chase for a third straight US Open semi-final when she faces fellow American Emma Navarro, who defeated Russian Anna Kalinskaya 6-4 6-2.

Earlier on Sunday, Noskova's sense of relief was cleared as she crouched to the ground after taking her sixth match point about an hour after earning her first.

The 21-year-old served for the match in the second set, but missed her first two match points as Kostyuk battled back from 5-3 down to force a decider.

Noskova failed to take her next two match points in the decider, while she missed her fifth match point after saving a break point, before finally getting over the line after an emotionally draining two and a half hours on court.

"I am more than relieved, this match was so tough, emotionally a bit more than physically," said Noskova, who missed five championship points before lifting the Wimbledon title this summer.

"Today was very close, it could have ended both ways. With all the chances I had in the second set, it was tough to still kind of restart."

In the women's doubles, British pair Harriet Dart and Maia Lumsden lost 6-2 6-2 to Spain's Cristina Bucsa and American Nicole Melichar-Martinez, the sixth seeds.
